title: Hail holy light, ofspring of Heav'n first-born
short: The invocation to Light, which may be the first created thing, an eternal emanation of God, or God himself: Milton deliberately leaves the question open.
body: The second invocation of the poem turns from Hell to Heaven. Milton offers three possible names for what he addresses: the 'ofspring of Heav'n first-born', created light (Genesis 1:3, where light is the first thing made); the 'Coeternal beam' of the Eternal, existing as long as God; or God himself, since 'God is light' (1 John 1:5) and dwells 'in the light which no man can approach unto' (1 Timothy 6:16). Verity sets out the alternatives and the scriptural texts. The caution of 'May I express thee unblam'd?' reflects Milton's heterodox theology: in his Christian Doctrine he denied that the Son was co-eternal with the Father, so the question of what light is touches the doctrine of the Trinity. Verity also notes how personal the passage is: light is what the blind poet has lost.

title: Escap't the Stygian Pool ... th' Orphean Lyre
short: The poet presents himself as returning from Hell like Orpheus or Aeneas, but singing with a holier inspiration than Orpheus' hymn to Night.
body: Having narrated Hell and Chaos (Books I-II), the poet describes himself as a traveller who has escaped the 'Stygian Pool', passed through 'utter' (outer) darkness and 'middle' darkness, and returned to light. Verity compares Dante's description of having risen from the 'lowest pool' of the universe (Paradiso 33.22-24). The 'Orphean Lyre' refers to the hymns attributed to the mythical singer Orpheus, which included one to Night; Orpheus descended to the underworld for Eurydice (Ovid, Metamorphoses 10) but failed to bring her back. Milton claims to have been taught by 'the heav'nly Muse' to 'venture down The dark descent, and up to reascend, Though hard and rare', which Verity identifies as an echo of the Sibyl's warning in Aeneid 6.126-29, already used at 2.432-33.

title: So thick a drop serene hath quencht thir Orbs
short: A translation of gutta serena, the medical term for the kind of blindness Milton suffered, in which the eyes look clear but cannot see.
body: 'Drop serene' renders the Latin gutta serena, the physicians' name for blindness without visible damage to the eye, in contrast to the 'dim suffusion' (suffusio, cataract) mentioned in the next line. The Dartmouth edition notes that Milton had been totally blind since about 1652, and that his eyes were said to look unclouded. 'Orbs' means eyeballs, as Verity notes, comparing Virgil's oculorum orbes (Aeneid 12.670). The passage is one of the most direct personal statements in the poem, and the identification of narrator and poet is here almost complete. Milton describes his blindness also in Sonnet 19 ('When I consider how my light is spent') and in the Second Defence of the English People (1654), where he denies that it was a divine punishment.

title: Thamyris, Maeonides, Tiresias and Phineus
short: Two blind poets and two blind prophets, with whom the blind Milton hopes to be equalled in renown as he is in fate.
body: Milton names four ancient figures who, like himself, were blind. Thamyris was the Thracian bard who boasted he could outsing the Muses and was blinded by them (Iliad 2.594-600); Maeonides is Homer, so called as son of Maeon or a native of Maeonia (Lydia), whose blindness was traditional (Verity). Tiresias is the blind seer of Thebes in Sophocles' Oedipus the King, whom Milton cited as the man whose blindness was his best illumination; Phineus the blind prophet-king of Thrace, tormented by the Harpies and freed by the Argonauts, with whom Milton compared himself in a letter to Leonard Philaras (1654). Verity notes that only the first two were poets: Milton hopes to equal them in 'renown' as well as fate. The nightingale that 'Sings darkling' (3.38-40) completes the picture of song in darkness.

title: the Book of knowledg fair ... a Universal blanc
short: For the blind poet the book of nature is a blank page; he prays instead for the celestial light to 'Shine inward'.
body: The image draws on the old idea of creation as God's second book, read alongside Scripture (the Dartmouth edition compares Calvin, Institutes 1.5). For Milton the 'Book of knowledg fair' is now 'a Universal blanc', its works 'expung'd and ras'd', and 'wisdom at one entrance quite shut out' (the eye being the gateway of knowledge). Verity notes the loose absolute construction of that line and its climax-like force. The turn that follows is the heart of the invocation: 'So much the rather thou Celestial light Shine inward', so that he may 'see and tell Of things invisible to mortal sight' (3.51-55). Physical blindness becomes the condition of prophetic vision, linking the poet to Tiresias and to the 'darkness visible' of the inverted world of Hell.

anchor: The radiant image of his Glory
title: The radiant image of his Glory
short: The Son, seated at the Father's right hand, is the visible image of the invisible God, a phrase taken from Hebrews 1:3.
body: The Son is described in the language of Hebrews 1:3, 'the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person', who 'sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high'; Verity cites the verse. In Milton's theology the Father is invisible (5.157; 3.375-77) and the Son is the means by which he is seen and through whom he acts, 'in whom the fulness dwels of love divine' (3.225). Satan's relation to Sin, who is 'thy perfect image' (2.764), is a deliberate parody. Milton's view that the Son was begotten in time, not eternally co-equal (Christian Doctrine 1.5), is a long-debated feature of the poem; C. S. Lewis held that its heresies are scarcely visible in the poem itself, while Maurice Kelley and others read the poem in the light of the treatise.

anchor: Sufficient to have stood, though free to fall
title: Sufficient to have stood, though free to fall
short: God's central defence: angels and humans were created able to stand, yet free; foreknowledge does not cause their fall.
body: The Father's speech (3.80-134) is the theological core of the poem's theodicy. Man was made 'just and right, Sufficient to have stood, though free to fall'; so were the angels. Without freedom, obedience would be no proof of 'true allegiance, constant Faith or Love'. God insists that his foreknowledge 'had no influence on their fault', and that 'Reason also is choice' (3.108), an idea the Dartmouth edition traces to Areopagitica ('reason is but choosing'). Verity quotes Christian Doctrine 1.3: God allowed men and angels to stand or fall by their own uncontrolled choice. The line has been both admired as a precise statement of the Arminian position and criticised for the defensive, legal tone of the speaker; Satan himself admits the point in soliloquy (4.66-68).

title: Self-tempted, self-deprav'd: Man falls deceiv'd
short: Why Man is offered grace and the fallen angels are not: they fell by their own suggestion, Man was deceived by another.
body: The distinction explains a central asymmetry of the poem. The 'first sort', the rebel angels, 'by thir own suggestion fell', where 'suggestion' has its old sense of temptation (Verity); they were self-tempted and self-corrupted, so no mercy is offered. Man falls 'deceiv'd By the other first', and 'therefore shall find grace'. The Dartmouth edition notes the complication that Book IX shows Adam falling 'not deceav'd' (9.998), echoing 1 Timothy 2:14 ('Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived was in the transgression'), so that the distinction applies most clearly to Eve. The principle that grace answers deception prepares for the Son's offer and for the repentance of Book X.

anchor: Some I have chosen of peculiar grace
title: Some I have chosen of peculiar grace
short: A carefully hedged statement of election: some are specially chosen, but grace is offered to all who will respond.
body: The lines on grace (3.173-202) set out a moderate, Arminian alternative to strict Calvinist predestination. Some are 'chosen of peculiar grace Elect above the rest', but the rest are not reprobate from eternity: they 'shall hear me call, and oft be warnd' and may 'safe arrive' if they persist. God will soften the 'stonie hearts' (Ezekiel 36:26, which Verity suggests is the source) and give them 'Umpire Conscience'. Only those who neglect the day of grace will be hardened. The Dartmouth edition notes that the repeated stress on human response departs from the Calvinism of many of Milton's republican associates. Critics debate whether 'peculiar grace' leaves a residue of unconditional election; Milton's Christian Doctrine (1.4) explicitly rejects reprobation decreed in advance.

title: Die hee or Justice must
short: The Father states the satisfaction theory of the atonement: Man's guilt must be paid for by death, his own or a willing substitute's.
body: The logic is legal: Man has broken his fealty and 'To expiate his Treason hath naught left'; 'Die hee or Justice must; unless for him Som other able, and as willing, pay The rigid satisfaction, death for death'. This is the theory of atonement as satisfaction of divine justice, associated with Anselm's Cur Deus Homo and developed by Reformation theologians. Verity notes the deliberate play on 'mortal' (deadly, and of mortals) in 'mortal crime' (3.215) and the echo, pointed out by Newton, of 1 Peter 3:18, 'the just for the unjust'. The Father's question 'Dwels in all Heaven charitie so deare?' is met by silence, which deliberately mirrors the silence of the devils when Beelzebub asks for a volunteer (2.417-26).

anchor: Behold mee then, mee for him
title: Behold mee then, mee for him, life for life
short: The Son volunteers to die for Man: the true heroic act of the poem, set against Satan's self-appointed mission in Book II.
body: In the silence of Heaven the Son offers himself: 'Behold mee then, mee for him, life for life I offer, on mee let thine anger fall'. The repetition of 'mee' gives the speech an urgency missing from the Father's legal argument. His sacrifice parallels and reverses Satan's offer to undertake the dangerous journey alone (2.430-66): the Dartmouth edition notes that Satan's 'one for all Myself expose' (2.827) parodies this voluntary sacrifice. The Son also prophesies his own victory over death, echoing 1 Corinthians 15:55 ('O death, where is thy sting?') and Psalm 16:10 ('thou wilt not leave my soul in hell'). The Father's response elevates the incarnate Son and promises that in the end 'God shall be All in All' (3.341; 1 Corinthians 15:28).

title: By Merit more then Birthright Son of God
short: The Son is exalted for what he has chosen to do, not merely for his birth: merit answers Satan's false claim to have been 'by merit rais'd'.
body: The Father declares that the Son 'hast been found By Merit more then Birthright Son of God', because 'in thee Love hath abounded more then Glory abounds'. The phrase invites comparison with Satan, 'by merit rais'd To that bad eminence' (2.5-6), and makes merit the ground of authority in Heaven as well as Hell, but true merit is self-giving. Verity links the passage to Philippians 2:6-11, where Christ, 'being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God' but humbled himself and was therefore exalted, and every knee shall bow. The emphasis on the Son's deserving rather than his nature fits Milton's subordinationist theology, as the Dartmouth edition notes; it also prepares for Satan's resentment of the Son's earlier exaltation in Book V.

title: Immortal Amarant
short: The legendary unfading flower: once grown in Eden, now transplanted to Heaven, it crowns the angels as they worship.
body: Amaranth takes its name from Greek amarantos, 'unfading'. Peter promises the faithful 'a crown of glory that fadeth not away' (1 Peter 5:4), where the Greek is amarantinos, 'amaranthine', which explains Milton's choice of flower for the angels' crowns. Verity glosses 'the unfading flower' and suggests that the idea of its removal from Paradise to Heaven 'when man offended' came from a rabbinical tradition that the garden itself was taken up to Heaven after the Fall. The angels cast their crowns before the throne, as the elders do in Revelation 4:10, and the river of bliss beside the 'Tree of Life' recalls Revelation 22:1-2. The unfading flower contrasts with the garland of roses Adam weaves for Eve in Book IX, which drops from his hand and fades the moment he learns of her fall (9.840-42, 892-93).

title: Dark with excessive bright
short: God's glory is so intense that it appears as darkness, and even the Seraphim veil their eyes with their wings.
body: In the angels' hymn God is 'Fountain of Light, thy self invisible', whose skirts appear 'Dark with excessive bright'. Verity calls the phrase an oxymoron that is also 'scientifically a fact', since overwhelming light blinds, and compares Drummond and Spenser for the same idea. The Seraphim, the brightest order, 'with both wings veil thir eyes', as in Isaiah's vision, where each seraph has six wings and 'with twain he covered his face' (Isaiah 6:2). The paradox forms a pair with Hell's 'darkness visible' (1.63) and with the blind poet's prayer that light should 'Shine inward' (3.51-52). It also reflects the theology of a hidden God, known through the Son, 'In whose conspicuous count'nance' he is seen (3.385-86).

anchor: As when a Vultur on Imaus bred
title: a Vultur on Imaus bred ... Sericana
short: Satan on the outer shell of the universe is like a vulture from the Himalaya flying to prey on lambs in India, alighting on the plains of China.
body: Satan, walking on the dark outer surface of the universe, is compared to a vulture bred on Imaus, the classical name for part of the Himalaya (Verity connects it with Sanskrit himavat, 'snowy'), that leaves the barren lands of the 'roving Tartar' to feed on lambs and kids in the valleys of the Ganges or Hydaspes (Jhelum). On the way it lands on the plains of Sericana (northern China), 'where Chineses drive With Sails and Wind thir canie Waggons light'. Verity cites Heylyn's Cosmography and later travellers on Chinese land-yachts. As Verity notes, every element fits: the vulture is Satan, the flock mankind, the barren plain the outer shell. The exotic detail of wind-driven carts suits a creature borne on the winds of the 'windie Sea of Land'.

title: The Limbo of Vanity, or Paradise of Fools
short: On the outer shell of the universe Milton places a satirical limbo for all vain things and vain people, borrowing Ariosto's lunar valley of lost things.
body: The 'Paradise of Fools' is a proverbial phrase (Verity cites Romeo and Juliet), which Milton turns into a place: a windy waste on the outside of the world, where all 'things transitorie and vain' and the souls of those who sought glory or Heaven by vain means are blown. Verity traces the idea to Ariosto's Orlando Furioso (canto 34), where Astolfo finds in a valley of the moon all things lost on earth; Milton had translated some of those lines in Of Reformation, and here insists the place is 'Not in the neighbouring Moon' as 'some have dreamd'. The limbo replaces the Catholic limbo of unbaptised infants and the patriarchs with a satire on superstition. The rubbish includes 'Reliques, Beads, Indulgences, Dispenses, Pardons, Bulls', blown away by a side-wind.

title: Empedocles and Cleombrotus
short: Two philosophers who sought immortality by suicide: Empedocles leapt into Etna to seem a god, Cleombrotus drowned himself after reading Plato's Phaedo.
body: Among the foolish seekers of heaven are Empedocles, the Sicilian philosopher of the fifth century BC, who by legend threw himself into the crater of Etna so that his disappearance would make men think him a god, but the volcano threw up one of his sandals (Verity; Horace tells the story in the Ars Poetica 463-66, as the Dartmouth edition notes); and Cleombrotus of Ambracia, who drowned himself after reading Plato's description of the soul's immortality in the Phaedo, so as to enjoy 'Plato's Elysium' at once. The Dartmouth note cites Lactantius (Divine Institutes 3.18) for Cleombrotus. The point is that a desire for transcendence pursued by one's own will, rather than through obedience, lands in the same windy limbo as monks and relic-hunters.

title: Eremits and Friers White, Black and Grey; Golgotha
short: Hermits and the mendicant orders, Carmelites (white), Dominicans (black) and Franciscans (grey), with pilgrims and those buried in friars' habits.
body: Milton's anti-Catholic satire is at its sharpest here. 'Eremits' are hermits (Greek erêmos, desert). Verity identifies the three orders by the colour of their habits: the Carmelites (White Friars), the Dominicans (Black Friars) and the Franciscans (Grey Friars). Pilgrims who 'stray'd so farr to seek In Golgotha him dead, who lives in Heav'n' are mocked for venerating the tomb of the risen Christ (Golgotha is the place of the crucifixion, Matthew 27:33). Those who 'Dying put on the weeds of Dominic, Or in Franciscan think to pass disguis'd' refer to the belief, noted by Masson (via Verity), that laymen buried in a friar's habit would gain heaven. At Heaven's 'wicket' St Peter with his keys (Matthew 16:19) waits in vain; the diminutive word is itself a sneer, as the Dartmouth edition observes.

anchor: The Stairs were such as whereon Jacob saw
title: The Stairs ... whereon Jacob saw Angels
short: A golden stair joins Heaven to the opening in the universe, like the ladder of Jacob's dream at Bethel, its steps carrying a mystical meaning.
body: Satan sees a stairway leading up to Heaven's gate, 'such as whereon Jacob saw Angels ascending and descending' when he fled from Esau to Padan-aram and slept at Luz, which he renamed Bethel (Genesis 28:10-19). Verity suggests that Jacob's dream gave Milton the idea of a stair connecting the universe with Heaven, and compares Dante's golden ladder in the heaven of Saturn (Paradiso 21). 'Each Stair mysteriously was meant': the steps were traditionally allegorised as the degrees of spiritual ascent. The stair is sometimes drawn up, 'whether to dare The Fiend by easie ascent, or aggravate His sad exclusion'. Directly below lies an opening down to earth, wider than the passage over Paradise, which Verity identifies as the only opening in the outer shell of the universe.

title: a spot like which perhaps Astronomer ... Through his glaz'd Optic Tube yet never saw
short: Satan alighting on the sun is a 'spot' such as Galileo's telescope never revealed: an allusion to the newly discovered sunspots.
body: Satan lands on the sun, a dark spot on its 'lucent Orbe' larger than any astronomer has seen. Verity takes the reference to be to Galileo, whose telescope ('optic tube', a common seventeenth-century word) revealed spots on the solar disc, and quotes Marvell's lines on 'spots unknown in the bright star descried'. Galileo's sunspot observations (published 1613) were controversial because they showed that the heavens, held to be perfect and unchanging, were blemished. The allusion therefore carries a moral charge: Satan is the first stain on the purity of the created heavens. The passage leads into an extended description of the sun's alchemical powers and its jewel-like substance, compared with the gems of Aaron's breastplate (Exodus 28:17-20).

title: that stone ... Volatil Hermes ... old Proteus
short: The sun as the 'Arch-chimic', true alchemist: what alchemists vainly seek, the philosopher's stone and elixir, the sun produces naturally.
body: The sun's substance may be the philosopher's stone that alchemists 'in vain so long have sought', the agent that would turn base metals to gold. Verity explains the jargon: to 'bind Volatil Hermes' is to fix mercury (quicksilver, named after Hermes/Mercury), and he cites Ben Jonson's masque Mercury Vindicated from the Alchemists. To 'call up unbound In various shapes old Proteus' alludes to the shape-shifting old man of the sea, who must be held fast until he returns to his true form (Odyssey 4.454-59; Virgil, Georgics 4.437-40); so the alchemists' matter passes through many forms in the 'Limbec' (alembic) until reduced to its 'native forme'. The 'Elixir' and 'Potable Gold' were supposed life-prolonging tinctures. Milton contrasts their vain art with the sun, 'th' Arch-chimic', which ripens gems and metals in the earth.

title: Uriel, one of the seav'n
short: The archangel stationed in the sun, one of the seven spirits before God's throne; his name means 'fire of God'.
body: Uriel does not appear in the canonical Bible; Verity notes that he is named in 2 Esdras (4:1, 4:36) and that Milton, in Christian Doctrine 1.9, identifies the seven angels who stand before God (Revelation 8:2; compare 1:4 and Zechariah 4:10) as those who traverse the earth on God's errands. His name, 'fire' or 'light of God', explains the tradition, cited by Verity from Heywood's Hierarchy of the Blessed Angels, that he governs the sun and the south; John too saw 'an angel standing in the sun' (Revelation 19:17). Satan, disguised as a 'stripling Cherube', deceives him with flattery and a show of devout curiosity, and Uriel directs him to Paradise. In Book IV Uriel detects him by his passions and warns Gabriel.

anchor: Hypocrisie, the only evil that walks
title: Hypocrisie, the only evil that walks Invisible, except to God alone
short: Uriel, sharpest-sighted of spirits, is deceived because hypocrisy is invisible to all but God, and goodness is slow to suspect.
body: The narrator's comment explains how 'the sharpest sighted Spirit of all in Heav'n' could be fooled: 'neither Man nor Angel can discern Hypocrisie', for 'goodness thinks no ill Where no ill seems'. Verity, following Newton, calls it a just allegory: a wise and noble nature is deceived precisely because it attributes its own honesty to others. The passage protects the good angels from the charge of negligence and prepares for Eve's deception in Book IX, where the same principle applies. It also clarifies the limits of angelic knowledge in the poem: only God is omniscient, and good angels, like humans, must act on what appears. Satan's power throughout depends on disguise, from the stripling cherub to the toad, cormorant and serpent.

title: Niphates top
short: A mountain of the Taurus range in Armenia, near the region where Milton places Eden; from it Satan first surveys the new world.
body: Satan descends from the sun and alights 'on Niphates top', a peak of the Taurus range in Armenia, as Verity and the Dartmouth edition note; Verity glosses the name as 'the snowy range'. Eden, in the geography Milton follows, lay in Mesopotamia between the Tigris and Euphrates, and Book IV opens with Satan gazing from this height towards Paradise and the sun, in the soliloquy that reveals his inner hell (4.32-113). The mountain thus becomes the first of the poem's places of temptation and survey; Milton later sets the Son's temptation in Paradise Regained (3.252-65) on a similar specular mount, and Michael shows Adam the future from 'a Hill Of Paradise the highest' (11.377-78).
